clue.text: Trader Mike in predicament with church spreading bombast

indicators.note: the bombast is spread apart to make room for the church

parts.note: a scrape = a predicament
Mike is M in the NATO alphabet, set inside SCRAPE: SCRAP(M)E

indicators.note: Mike goes inside the predicament

parts.note: rant = bombastic talk
standard abbreviation, set inside RANT: R(CH)ANT

explanation.surface: A dealer called Mike is in trouble with a church that is full of hot air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spreading' reads as the church spreading its message, but it means the bombast is pulled apart so the church can sit inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrap merchant is a trader who buys and sells scrap.

clue.text: Complaint from south Taipei came unexpectedly

parts.note: standard abbreviation

indicators.note: the letters turn up in an unexpected order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: Someone lodges a complaint after a trip south to Taipei came as a surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' reads as a grievance, but it means an illness, as in 'a stomach complaint'.
explanation.definitionFit: Septicaemia is blood poisoning, a serious medical complaint.

clue.text: Verse in song of praise briefly adopted by army corps

indicators.note: the corps takes the shortened hymn in, as a family adopts a child

parts.note: RE = Royal Engineers, the army corps
a hymn is a song of praise; 'briefly' docks its last letter, and the rest goes inside RE

explanation.surface: An army corps takes up a hymn, verse and all.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Engineers (RE) are the crossword's usual army corps.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyme can mean verse in general, as in 'nursery rhyme'.

clue.text: Seemingly ceaseless repeat Rumpole regularly broadcast

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so the letters are taken at a steady every-other step
the letters are scattered widely, like seed

parts.note: anagram fodder, used as it stands
the 2nd, 4th and 6th letters of rUmPoLe

explanation.surface: A TV repeat of Rumpole of the Bailey seems to be on forever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' fits the TV picture so well that it hides its job of mixing the letters. Rumpole of the Bailey is a long-running British TV legal drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Something perpetual goes on, or seems to go on, without end.

clue.text: European going on vacation with only half of blasted drink

indicators.note: emptied out, so only the outer letters of the word remain
keep only the first half of the eight-letter oath

parts.note: flipping is a mild British oath meaning blasted

explanation.surface: A European leaving on holiday with half of a cursed drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going' emptied leaves GG; FLIPPING, the British euphemism for blasted, halved leaves FLIP.
explanation.definitionFit: An egg flip is a hot drink of beaten egg with milk or ale and sugar, a kind of nog.

clue.text: Clergy unwilling to be led by agnostic's conclusion

indicators.note: a word's conclusion is where it ends, so only its final letter is used
the last letter goes in front

parts.note: last letter of agnostiC
loth = unwilling, a variant of loath

explanation.surface: Clergy are reluctant to follow the lead of an agnostic's reasoning.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface puts clergy and an agnostic at odds, which keeps 'the cloth' out of mind.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The cloth' is the clergy, from their distinctive dress.

clue.text: Complain bitterly about being shown up following software evaluation

indicators.note: the complaint wraps around the next piece

parts.note: an app is a piece of software

indicators.note: the rest comes after the software

parts.note: to rail = to complain bitterly

indicators.note: in a down answer, the piece reads upwards

parts.note: AS (= being, as in 'as a child') turned upwards, set inside RAIL: RAI(SA)L

explanation.surface: Someone moans after a software review made them look bad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being' stands for AS ('as / being a child, I…'), and 'shown up' looks like embarrassment but turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a staff appraisal is a formal evaluation of someone's work.

clue.text: Cask enthusiast rolled over

indicators.note: the word is turned over, reading backwards

parts.note: a nut = a fan, as in 'fitness nut'

explanation.surface: A beer lover's barrel is rolled across the cellar floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolled over' suits a barrel, which is what the answer is.
explanation.definitionFit: A tun is a large cask for wine or beer.

clue.text: Nimble mole checking run

indicators.note: the mole holds back, and so holds in, the run

parts.note: a mole is a spy inside an organisation
cricket scoring abbreviation, which goes inside the mole's letters

explanation.surface: A quick-footed mole stops someone making a run for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mole' is the burrowing animal in the surface and the planted spy in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Spry means nimble and lively, especially of an older person.

clue.text: Post-defeat, again rallying Germany about call involving press

indicators.note: the call wraps around the press

parts.note: abbreviation for Germany

indicators.note: Germany's abbreviation is turned about

parts.note: to ring = to call on the phone
Oxford University Press, set inside RING: R(OUP)ING

explanation.surface: After a loss, Germany's side regroups around a rallying call, with the press involved.
explanation.walkthrough: OUP is Oxford University Press, a publisher the Times uses as 'press'.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: an army that regroups gathers its scattered forces to rally after a setback.

clue.text: Coveted property pair has left in excellent Suffolk village

indicators.note: in here means set within, so the shortened prize sits inside the word for excellent

parts.note: swell is dated slang for excellent

indicators.note: has left means the pair letters depart from the word for coveted property

parts.note: a prize is something coveted, a desirable possession

explanation.surface: A sought-after house in a lovely Suffolk village loses its owners, a couple who moved away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pair has left' reads as a couple moving out; it is the abbreviation PR leaving. Sizewell is a coastal village in Suffolk, an English county, known for its nuclear power station.
explanation.definitionFit: Sizewell is a hamlet on the Suffolk coast, home to a nuclear power station.

clue.text: Tries ecstasy, the ultimate transport for some?

parts.note: a court hears, that is tries, a case
E = the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Someone tries ecstasy, as the ultimate trip for some partygoers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimate' is the joke: a hearse is the final vehicle anyone rides in. The question mark flags that the definition is playful.
explanation.definitionFit: A hearse is the last vehicle many of us will ride in.

clue.text: Novel form of alarm sirens

indicators.note: the letters take a new form

parts.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

explanation.surface: A new kind of alarm siren has been invented.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' reads as the adjective 'new', but it is the noun: a book.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: George Eliot's 1861 book about a miserly weaver is one novel among many.

clue.text: Notorious meal in most unsuitable boozer

parts.note: the last = the least suitable, as in 'the last person I'd ask'
one who sups, that is drinks

explanation.surface: A dreadful meal is served in the worst pub imaginable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boozer' is British slang for a pub, which the surface uses, but here it is a drinker: one who sups.
explanation.definitionFit: The Last Supper, Jesus's final meal with his disciples, is the most famous meal in history.

clue.text: Four-letter word, eg "tart", deplorably supported by beastly male

indicators.note: in a down light a piece supported by another sits on top of it
deplorably means in a shocking way, so the letters of eg and tart are put in disorder

parts.note: a ram is a male sheep, a male beast

explanation.surface: A rude four-letter word for a woman, said by a brutish man.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests 'tart' itself is the four-letter word; in fact EG and TART together rearrange to TETRAG, with RAM underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: A tetragram is any word of four letters; the Greek prefix tetra means four.

clue.text: Trots round public leisure area with yellow covers?

indicators.note: the Trots go round the rest

parts.note: Trotskyists, left-wingers, are reds

indicators.note: the yellow joins the leisure area

parts.note: the rec, a recreation ground, set inside REDS
or = gold/yellow in heraldry; it follows the rec inside the Trots

explanation.surface: Joggers run round a park wearing yellow waterproofs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covers' looks like the joggers' clothing; it is songs another artist records again. A rec is British for a public playing field.
explanation.definitionFit: A band that covers a song re-records it in its own version.

clue.text: Leaving hotel, family lying about identity

indicators.note: the hotel is left behind, so its letter departs from the word
what remains lies the other way round

parts.note: FLESH (as in 'flesh and blood', family) without H for hotel

explanation.surface: A family skips out on a hotel bill after lying about who they are.
explanation.walkthrough: H is Hotel in the NATO alphabet. 'Lying about' reads as dishonesty but turns the letters round.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: your sense of self is your sense of who you are.

clue.text: Initially Sweep, a dog, snubbed Sooty? This could be so

indicators.note: the first letter of the next word
cut short, so the last letter of the dog is lost

parts.note: a mutt is a mongrel dog

explanation.surface: Sweep, the puppet dog, cold-shoulders his partner Sooty, the puppet bear from British children's television.
explanation.walkthrough: Sooty and Sweep are puppets on a British children's show; here sooty is the adjective, and the definition is the whole closing phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Smut is soot or a flake of grime, which makes whatever it lands on dirty and blackened.

clue.text: Vulgar, lawless half of crowd's rioting

indicators.note: a riot is wild disorder, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written into the mix

indicators.note: the first half, three of its six letters

parts.note: the word crowds, read without its apostrophe

explanation.surface: A rough, lawless section of a crowd running riot.
explanation.definitionFit: Lower-class is used snobbishly to mean common or unrefined, coarse in manner.

clue.text: Perhaps one who quickly moves a tiny distance

definitions.meaning: one who whisks things away, a made-up agent noun
the tiny margin by which a race is won

explanation.surface: Someone darting about only ever covers a short distance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' warns that WHISKER as 'one who whisks' is a whimsical coinage, not a dictionary sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A whisker is a very small margin, and a whisker is also someone who whisks.

clue.text: Bears receiving treats every so often as bait

indicators.note: the word takes the letters in

parts.note: has = bears, as in 'bears a name'

indicators.note: take letters at intervals

parts.note: the 2nd, 4th and 6th letters of tReAtS, received inside the word for bears

explanation.surface: Bears are lured with treats scattered about as bait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bears' looks like the animals being tempted; it is the verb. 'Bait' is the verb too: to torment.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from bear-baiting: setting dogs on a chained bear to torment it.

clue.text: Delivered fine cut

indicators.note: the word is spoken, as a speech is delivered

parts.note: sheer = fine, as of a thin fabric

explanation.surface: A fine cut of meat has been delivered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivered' looks like a courier's word, but it means spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, most familiar from sheep being sheared of their fleece.

clue.text: Gradually winch me aloft, but not to the full extent

indicators.text: but not to the full extent
indicators.note: only part of the words is used

parts.note: the letters run across the three words, dropping the first and last two

explanation.surface: Someone asks to be hoisted up slowly, and not all the way.
explanation.walkthrough: Inchmeal is an old word meaning 'inch by inch'. The surface of being winched up slowly fits the definition exactly.
explanation.definitionFit: Inchmeal means gradually, little by little.

clue.text: Fighter protects revolutionary British gangland boss, say

indicators.note: the fighter surrounds, guarding, the letters

parts.note: a MiG is a Russian fighter plane

indicators.note: the abbreviation is turned round

parts.note: BR (British) turned round, then protected inside the fighter

explanation.surface: A hired fighter guards a British revolutionary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like a noun for a rebel; it is an adjective saying 'turn this round'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Big is the nickname for the head of a criminal gang.

clue.text: RIP, weightlifter? Sentimental stuff

parts.note: a rip = a tear
one who lifts a weight with the jerk, as in the clean and jerk

explanation.surface: A gravestone for a weightlifter, the kind of thing that brings on a sob.
explanation.walkthrough: RIP is capitalised to suggest 'rest in peace' and a death; in the wordplay it is just a rip.
explanation.definitionFit: A tear-jerker is a sentimental film or story made to make you cry.

clue.text: Journalist bagging last of lion's share

indicators.note: the journalist puts the letter in a bag, that is contains it

parts.note: ED = editor

indicators.note: the last of anything is its final part, here the final letter of the word

parts.note: last letter of lioN, bagged by the journalist

explanation.surface: A reporter grabs the lion's share of the credit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lion's share' is a set phrase that pulls 'share' into the wordplay; it is the definition. One's end of a deal is one's share.
explanation.definitionFit: Your end of a deal is your share of it, as in 'keep up your end'.

clue.text: Live next-door to new unknown engineer

parts.note: to be = to live, exist
standard abbreviation
algebra's unknowns are x, y and z

explanation.surface: Someone lives next door to a mysterious new engineer.
explanation.walkthrough: Karl Benz was the German engineer who built the first practical motor car.
explanation.definitionFit: Karl Benz was a German automotive engineer.

clue.text: UK business magnate having previously made rare volatile crystalline product

indicators.note: the magnate comes after the rearranged letters, which stand before him
volatile means unstable, so these letters are reformed in a new order

parts.note: Alan Sugar, the British entrepreneur of The Apprentice

explanation.surface: A British tycoon who earlier made something rare and unstable.
explanation.definitionFit: Demerara is a coarse light-brown cane sugar with large crystals, named after a region of Guyana.
